summary: This document describes issues of multi-tenancy in large data center networks and how overlay-based network virtualization may address them. Key needs include traffic isolation between tenants and address space isolation so different tenants can reuse the same addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: Many families live in one apartment building, and each wants private rooms and their own room numbers. This RFC explains the problem of giving each customer a private network inside shared data centers.

subtitle: Why large multi-tenant data centers need virtual networks, and why overlays are a good way to build them.

tldr.problem: Multi-tenant data centers need isolated virtual networks with their own address spaces, and VMs that can be placed and moved anywhere, which physical network designs handle poorly.
tldr.mechanism: An overlay encapsulates each packet at a first-hop Network Virtualization Edge (NVE), tunnels it over the IP underlay to the egress NVE, and uses a mapping system to know where each VM lives.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is the problem statement for the NVO3 working group; it identifies control-plane and data-plane work areas and reviews related technologies.

facts.label: Working group
facts.value: NVO3, overlays over an IP (L3) underlay

today: RFC 7364 is an Informational problem statement and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. It uses the terminology of RFC 7365, the companion framework document.

sections.title: Multi-Tenant Data Centers
sections.content:
Data centers are being consolidated and outsourced. With server virtualization, each physical server runs multiple virtual machines (VMs). A tenant is the administrative entity for whom virtual network instances are managed: a company for a public provider, or a department in an internal data center.

Tenants expect their traffic never to be exposed to others except through controlled interfaces such as a firewall. To a tenant, a virtual network looks like a normal Ethernet or L3 network whose only end stations are that tenant's. One tenant may have several virtual network instances.

Two issues come first: address space separation between tenants, and the ability to place and migrate VMs anywhere without matching the subnet boundaries of the underlying network. This is the problem statement for the Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) working group, which targets overlays over an IP underlay.
sections.plainLanguage: One building, many families. Each family wants a private floor that behaves like its own house.

sections.title: The Problem Areas
sections.content:
The RFC lists several problems.

  • Dynamic provisioning: properties like QoS are hard to keep when services move around.
  • VM mobility: a live-migrated VM needs to keep its IP and MAC addresses, but servers get addresses tied to their location, so VMs can only move within a subnet.
  • Forwarding table size: location independence pushes host routes such as /32 in IPv4 or per-VM MAC addresses into switches, possibly hundreds per server.
  • Logical and physical coupling: spreading a virtual network across racks or pods can need complex reconfiguration and conflict with bounding broadcast domains.
  • Address separation: tenants must be able to reuse addresses, and not collide with the underlay's.
  • Optimal forwarding: after a VM moves, the best gateway may change, and middleboxes with session state complicate this.
sections.plainLanguage: If every family had to keep its room number tied to one hallway, moving would be a mess and the front desk's list would get huge.

sections.title: How Network Overlays Work
sections.content:
Virtual networks isolate address spaces and limit the scope of packets: traffic leaves or enters only through controlled points such as a security gateway.

Each virtual network instance is an overlay. The first-hop device, a Network Virtualization Edge (NVE), encapsulates the original packet and tunnels it to a remote NVE. The rest of the network forwards based on the outer header and can ignore the payload. This is called "map-and-encap", with three steps: map the destination address to the egress NVE's underlay IP address, encapsulate, and forward by the underlay using the outer address, after which the egress NVE decapsulates and delivers.

The NVE can be a switch, router or a hypervisor's virtual switch. If a VM moves, the NVEs just update their mapping tables. Traffic between virtual networks, or to non-virtualized networks, goes through gateways. The overlay header carries a virtual network identifier, and the inner packet can be an Ethernet frame or an IP packet.
sections.plainLanguage: You put your letter in a bigger envelope addressed to the right building's mailroom. The post office reads only the big envelope, and the mailroom opens it.

sections.title: Design Characteristics and Work Areas
sections.content:
Overlays must suit highly distributed systems with many thousands of access switches, many virtual networks with sparse membership, and highly dynamic tenant systems. They should be incrementally deployable, work with existing operations (without requiring multicast beyond link-local scope, though able to use it), and operate within a single administrative domain.

The control plane has three work areas: the Network Virtualization Authority (NVA) that holds mapping information, the protocol NVEs use to talk to the NVA, and the attach and detach of VMs to a virtual network instance. The NVA could be a replicated directory database or an extended routing protocol such as BGP or IS-IS. In the data plane, many encapsulations already exist, and the RFC sees no need for yet another one just for NVO3.
sections.plainLanguage: The overlay needs a phone book (the NVA), a way for mailrooms to look things up in it, and a way to tell it when a family moves in or out.

sections.title: Related Work and Security
sections.content:
The RFC reviews BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, BGP/MPLS Ethernet VPNs, 802.1 VLANs, Shortest Path Bridging, VDP, ARMD, TRILL, L2VPNs, Proxy Mobile IP and LISP. It does not compare them. Notably, C-VLAN, S-VLAN and B-VLAN IDs are 12 bits, while the 24-bit I-SID allows more than 16 million virtual networks.

On security, the document introduces no risks itself, but solutions must address data-plane and control-plane concerns: isolation between virtual networks, spoofing, snooping, transit modification and denial of service, and protection of the control protocol from unauthorized parties.
sections.plainLanguage: Other people have built bits of this already, and the RFC lists them. Whatever is chosen has to keep each family's floor private and the mailroom list safe from tampering.
